paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) used exome and candidate panel sequencing in 2 unrelated children with epileptic encephalopathy. Both children carried the same de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GRIN2D gene, c.1999G-A, which causes a val667-to-ile (V667I) substitution. The substituted residue lies in the M3 transmembrane domain, which is involved in channel gating. Functional studies showed that the mutation caused a gain of function. It doubled glutamate and glycine potency and raised channel open probability 6-fold. It also reduced the receptor's sensitivity to negative modulators such as extracellular protons and prolonged deactivation after glutamate was removed.

paragraphs.text: Tsuchida et al. (2018) used whole-exome sequencing in 3 unrelated patients with severe developmental delay and intractable epilepsy. Each patient carried a novel heterozygous missense variant in the GRIN2D gene. The affected residues were highly conserved across vertebrates and among the 4 GluN2 subunits. From the protein structure, the authors predicted that all 3 variants probably impair GluN2D function, either by affecting how the subunits interact or by altering channel gating.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) tested the mutant receptors in vitro for sensitivity to FDA-approved NMDA receptor antagonists. They then gave oral memantine to both of their patients, and seizure burden and development improved mildly to moderately. The older proband later developed refractory status epilepticus, which improved dramatically on ketamine and magnesium. The authors suggested that NMDA receptor antagonists could be useful as adjuvant therapy in patients with GRIN2D gain-of-function mutations.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) found a de novo heterozygous c.1999G-A transition in the GRIN2D gene, causing a val667-to-ile (V667I) substitution, in 2 unrelated children with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-46 (DEE46). Their seizures did not respond to conventional antiepileptic medications. The mutation was found by exome and candidate panel sequencing. The substitution lies in the M3 transmembrane domain, which is involved in channel gating. Functional studies showed a gain of function: glutamate and glycine potency doubled, channel open probability rose 6-fold, sensitivity to negative modulators such as extracellular protons fell, and deactivation after glutamate removal was prolonged. Cultured neurons transfected with the mutant cDNA showed dendritic swelling and cell death.
